extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers, economists of innovation, patent scholars, patent policymakers, and patent attorneys analyzing continuation practice
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical evaluation of U.S. continuation patents (CAP, CIP, Division, Combination) and the firm- and patent-level metrics that characterize their use and value; includes econometric modeling of continuation choice and policy (post-1995) effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: CIPs produce patents with 26% more claims than 'ordinary' patents, reflecting their use by applicants to bring in additional material in the form of new claims. Divisional patents have significantly fewer claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the count of claims as an indicator of whether applicants used continuation-in-part to add material; higher claims count can signal insertion of additional subject matter (CIP) while low claims in Divisions may reflect carve-outs responded to restriction requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forward citations (4-year window) as value measure
rubrics_metrics.description: CIPs receive the highest number of forward citations within four years of issue (mean 2.7 citations/patent vs 2.3 in control sample, p<0.001). Divisional patents have significantly fewer forward citations; CAPs are associated with below-average forward citations (especially post-1995).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forward citations within a fixed window (here four years) are used as a proxy for patent quality/value. Compare continuation types and pre/post policy periods using the same citation window to reduce truncation bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of backward citations
rubrics_metrics.description: The average CAP patent has a significantly larger average number of backward citations; continued patents contain 50% more references to patented prior art (mostly attributable to applicants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count of backward citations can indicate how much prior art is being folded into the prosecution history (applicant-added citations matter); also note correlation with originality measures and technology-specific examiner practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion of backward self-citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-1995 CAPs contain a significantly higher proportion of backward self-citations than any other group; high proportion of backward self-cites may indicate a strategy of accumulating overlapping patents ('thickets').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the share of backward citations that cite the assignee's prior patents as a diagnostic of defensive/thicket-building strategies versus genuinely novel referencing; compare across continuation types and time periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renewal/expiration rates (short-term survival)
rubrics_metrics.description: CIPs are less likely to expire after 4 years of issue compared to 'ordinary' patents; Divisional patents have lower renewal rates by comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early renewal/maintenance behavior is a revealed-preference proxy for private value: patents that are renewed are more likely to be valuable. Use multi-year renewal/expiration statistics to infer private economic value differences across continuation types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pendency duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Continued patents pend for twice as long as patents without continuations in their review history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pendency (time in prosecution) is a key measure of the timing/strategic use of continuations (e.g., CAP extends pendency without substantial changes). When evaluating continuations, explicitly measure pendency differences versus non-continuation patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality measure (correlated with backward refs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'originality' measure is highly directly correlated with the number of backward references; the paper's 'originality' result holds even after controlling for the number of backward citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret originality indices in light of their correlation with backward citation counts. Analysts should control for backward citation numbers when using derived originality measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology-class continuation intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of continuations varies by technology: continuations accounted for 46% of patents in 'Drugs and Medicine' and 36% in 'Chemicals' (1981–2000). CIPs and Combinations dominate in Drugs & Chemicals; CAPs account for ~50% of continuations in Computers & Communications; semiconductors have high Divisional propensity (~40%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare continuation-type shares within technology classes; technological context strongly conditions continuation use and interpretation of metrics (value, citations, examiner behavior).

rubrics_metrics.name: Firm patenting intensity (PATINT)
rubrics_metrics.description: PATINT is measured as the ratio of a firm's patent applications that issue to R&D expenditures (annual); hypothesis: more patent-intensive firms are more likely to rely on continuations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include PATINT as a predictor of continuation propensity and interact with other firm-level variables to test theories (e.g., technology traders vs defensive patenters).

rubrics_metrics.name: R&D intensity (RDINT)
rubrics_metrics.description: RDINT is R&D expenditures normalized by employment; high RDINT interacting with PATINT is interpreted as indicating 'technology traders' or specialist R&D firms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use RDINT to distinguish firms that rely on patents as part of innovation strategy; positive PATINT x RDINT interaction predicted to increase probability of CIP filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital intensity (CAPINT / sunk-costs)
rubrics_metrics.description: CAPINT proxies sunk costs via book value of plant, property and equipment normalized by employment. Firms with high CAPINT and PATINT are characterized as 'defensive patenters'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use CAPINT and its interaction with PATINT to test whether firms adopt defensive continuation strategies (expect positive association with CAPs and Divisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent quality (firm-level forward citations / FCITES)
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality of an invention is proxied by forward citations received within 4 years of issue (FCITES); used both as direct predictor and in interaction terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include FCITES to capture patent importance; interactions (e.g., PATINT x CAPINT x FCITES) indicate whether continuations correlate with higher- or lower-value inventions for particular firm types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction: PATINT x RDINT (technology-trader indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: A positive coefficient for the interaction of patent-intensity and R&D-intensity supports the 'technology traders' characterization and predicts higher likelihood of certain continuation types (CIPs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret significant positive interaction as evidence that R&D-intensive, patent-intensive firms favor continuations consistent with pioneering/patent-trading motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction: PATINT x CAPINT (defensive-patenter indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: A positive coefficient for the interaction of patent-intensity and capital-intensity implies 'defensive patenters' and predicts higher CAP (and Division) probabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this interaction to test defensive patent accumulation hypotheses; examine its effect across technology sectors because sectoral patterns differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triple interaction: PATINT x CAPINT x FCITES (value mediation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The multiplicative interaction of patent-intensity, capital-intensity and patent value (FCITES) tests whether defensive patenters’ continuations are associated with lower or higher average patent quality — a negative coefficient implies lower quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreting triple interactions requires careful marginal-effect calculations (cross-derivatives); report changes in predicted probabilities for representative covariate changes (e.g., ±½ SD) to aid interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: TECHSHARE (centrality of patent to firm portfolio)
rubrics_metrics.description: TECHSHARE is the share of a patent's technology class in the firm's annual flow of patents (bounded at 1). Patents central to a firm's portfolio are more likely to use continuations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use TECHSHARE to control for a patent's fit with a firm's technological focus; higher TECHSHARE increases likelihood of continuation use across types.

rubrics_metrics.name: TECHTIME (patenting experience in class)
rubrics_metrics.description: TECHTIME is the difference between a patent's application year and the year the firm was first assigned a patent in that class; the longer TECHTIME is, the less likely a patent is to be continued (uniformly negative effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use TECHTIME to measure recency of a firm's activity in a technology area; more recent entrants (smaller TECHTIME) are more likely to use continuations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firm size (EMP) effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Firm size measured as log employment; size is inversely related to CIP filings but positively correlated with CAPs and Divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include firm size as a control: larger firms have economies of scale in prosecution and in-house counsel which affects continuation choices differently by type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firm age (AGE) as control
rubrics_metrics.description: Firm age (log) is included to distinguish effects due to experience and learning not captured by firm size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat AGE as a control variable when testing firm-attribute hypotheses about continuation use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multinomial logit (MNL) choice-model specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuation choice (j = {0=no continuation, 1=CAP, 2=CIP, 3=Divisional, 4=Combination}) is modeled with a multinomial logit; coefficients are interpreted relative to the no-continuation baseline. Effects are nonlinear and depend on covariate values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate by maximum likelihood and report marginal changes (e.g., change from -½ SD to +½ SD) to aid interpretation of interaction and nonlinear effects; be cautious interpreting raw coefficients due to nonlinearity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy-change (1995 patent-term) effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The 1995 change to 20 years from application (from 17 years from issue) coincides with a decline in CAPs and a decline in CAP patent quality post-1995; analyses should probe pre/post differences in continuation use and patent quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating continuations over time, explicitly model or stratify pre- and post-1995 periods and control for truncation and procedural changes; do not ascribe causality to the term change without addressing confounders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural classification confounding (FWC/CPA/RCE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural changes (File Wrapper Continuations (FWC) pre-1995, Continued Prosecution Application (CPA) introduced with 1995 changes, and later Request for Continued Examination (RCE)) alter how continued prosecution is recorded; pre-1995 CAP counts may include items later classified differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for CPA/FWC/RCE conflation when comparing continuation frequencies across periods; control for differing inclusion rules to avoid measurement error in continuation counts and quality comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firm-type characterization: 'technology traders' vs 'defensive patenters'
rubrics_metrics.description: Two interpretations of continuation use: (a) 'technology traders' (specialists with high R&D and patent intensity) use continuations (esp CIPs) for pioneering inventions; (b) 'defensive patenters' (high capital- and patent-intensity) use continuations (esp CAPs and Divisions) to amass portfolios for cross-licensing and defense. Empirical signatures: CIPs associated with high-value patents and small R&D-intensive firms; CAPs associated with low-value patents, high backward self-cites, and large patent-intensive firms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use combinations of PATINT, RDINT, CAPINT, FCITES, TECHSHARE, TECHTIME, size and self-citation measures to distinguish these archetypes, but recognize the paper's caution that statistical tests alone cannot definitively pin down motives without additional data (licensing, litigation, R&D composition).
